$comment: Cases both editors must judge alike. Each case is a source and the issues expected for it, sorted by start, end and code; offsets count UTF-16 code units. An issue without start and end is checked by code only: the two JavaScript parsers do not always place a syntax error on the same character. fixes holds the whole source after each quick fix, in the order offered. The severity and message, where a case gives them, are checked as well.

issues.message: Datastar rewrites $b in a string into $['b'], because its pattern pairs the quotes before it differently. The ' it writes ends the string, so the browser cannot parse the expression.

cases.name: a signal in a double-quoted string the client opens elsewhere, which then holds the rewrite

issues.message: Datastar rewrites $b in a string into $['b'], because its pattern pairs the quotes before it differently, so the string holds that.

cases.name: a dollar and a digit in the text of a template literal

issues.message: Datastar rewrites $5 in a template literal into $['5'], because the literal also holds a ${...}, so the text holds that. To keep the text, write ${'$'}5 or put the text in a quoted string, which Datastar leaves as written.

cases.name: a signal in the text of a template literal, said with both ways out

issues.message: Datastar rewrites $total in a template literal into $['total'], because the literal also holds a ${...}, so the text holds that. Write ${$total} for the signal's value. To keep the text, write ${'$'}total or put the text in a quoted string, which Datastar leaves as written.

cases.name: a quote in a comment, said with the quote the client pairs

issues.message: Datastar does not rewrite $b: its pattern takes the ' in a comment before it for the start of a string, and leaves everything up to the next ' as written. The browser reads $b as a JavaScript variable, not as the signal.

cases.name: a slash inside a class of a regular expression, which does not end it
